utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. If I can ask the representative of the registry to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. John Ostojic along with Danilo Cirkovic on behalf of Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we hopefully can conclude Witness DD, let me ask what about the list for the witnesses to be called the first -- yes, the first eight days in January. This list was due today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, and we have the list here that we can distribute to the Court and to the OTP. However, just as a matter of reference or note, it is just a single-page list. We would ask that it be kept confidential, because at this point there are some within this list that may be seeking protective measures and some that have, but what we've done is identified them by the number from our 65 ter disclosures as well as their full name. So if I can just apply for that cautionary measure to be utilised for these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. I think there are no objections. It may be treated confidential until further notice. And I take it that the proffers for these witnesses have been distributed? For example, number 15 was on the list of missing proffers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's my understanding that now the OTP is in possession of all the proffers for those witnesses that we've just submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As you know, also the Judges are extremely grateful if we have the proffers, and we missed until now number 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's also my understanding, Your Honour, that we've submitted the proffers to be delivered to the Court as well. We can -- we can verify that. And if not, we'll get it at the next break to secure that the Court has it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently it was distributed right now. Then any other additional issues? It was my understanding that the order of appearances should change during this week. Correct? Especially for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That is accurate, Your Honour. And if I can just explain. It's not necessarily a change, but when we anticipate a certain length of time for a witness, we cannot and do not anticipate the length of time that the OTP will undertake to cross. So our schedule is based on our best guesstimate, if you will, and we had scheduled today's witnesses, but obviously we're still on Witness 05, DD, and the following witness will be as scheduled in the same order, which is Witness number 44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who also, if I'm not incorrect, the Court has granted protective measures, both pseudonym, facial distortion, and voice distortion. He'll proceed next in the order that we suggested. Following Witness 044, we will be calling Witness number 052, whose name is Vladimir Makovski. He is not -- is not seeking protective measures, and that's why I identify him also by his name and number. Following Mr. Makovski, the Defence will call Witness number 045. We do not anticipate asking for protective measures for Witness 045, however, I have not in detail discussed with this witness his desires, if any, regarding that, so I'd prefer not to identify him at this moment. But I don't anticipate that we will be seeking those measures for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So those three witnesses for the remainder of the week we think will adequately fulfil the time period -- or at least we anticipate that it will, especially given or in light of the first witness, DD, having taken the time that it did, which is -- we're not objecting it to, obviously. We welcome it. And we think that that will be all the witnesses we will call for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You indicated earlier that there would be an additional two witnesses. And we have tomorrow and we have Friday. The plenary for Friday has been cancelled, but this Trial Chamber will continue and is ready to hear the witnesses that are present in The Hague. It should never be the case that we send a witness home without having heard the witness. So therefore, please take care that the witnesses still stay in The Hague and we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm in agreement to proceed. I think that we'll take up the entire period of the week with the remaining three witnesses, however. With respect to Witness number 71, he's not coming to The Hague. He is not in The Hague. And we will not be calling him this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then the final one? There was one in addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think the Court is referring to Witness number 68 68. There were some personal problems that had arisen with respect to Witness number 68. We are trying to get all the information in connection with this witness. We will be to inform the Court more fully on that hopefully later this evening or tomorrow morning in connection with his personal circumstances that I've discussed with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But the witness is in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That witness is, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in principle, we expect to hear also Witness number 086 from the 65 ter list. But in future, we should make reference only to the final Defence list prepared by the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, Your Honour, 086 is not at The Hague, but 068 is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, the record says that you're requesting 086 on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And it's 068. I don't want to mention the name, 3rd March birthday. Correct? Okay. Anything in addition?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, if I may, since I have the floor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, a matter arose yesterday in questioning by the Court, and I would just like some guidance on it if I may. With all due respect to the Court, the Court asked a witness a question. It is not my practice, if you will, to object unless I feel that it is of utmost necessity, particularly with respect to the OTP witnesses. My question, if the Court would be kind enough to assist me in understanding it, relates to the question Your Honour asked whether Keraterm was similarly or was it known to be the same type of institution as Omarska in 1992. With all due respect to the Court, 1992 in August, as we all know, the international press uncovered Omarska and Keraterm as well as Trnopolje. There was much media in 1992 after that. I don't want to utilise the answer given by the witness, although I'll obviously -- it's the Court's discretion to advise us, hopefully, on this, to suggest that that was known to this individual prior or after certain dates. I think the individual answered the question. There was some perhaps confusion, and he answered it in the affirmative. I would ask if it's necessary for the Court to determine whether this witness knew, since he was not ever physically at Keraterm, based on his testimony, but did visit Omarska once and Trnopolje on three separate occasions that, if the Court wishes, I can ask that if I'm given an opportunity on redirect or just to clarify it. Because I think as the transcript reads now, it's left too broad for interpretation. Again, I say with the most respect. It is just -- we're looking for guidance and dates and times are extremely important for us, I think as the Court has gathered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be for the Defence if they are not satisfied with the one or other answer and they might feel that an answer was ambiguous to address this issue in the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So that's the reason why we proceeded this way before you started your re-examination. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There is one other point, if I may, for the record, Your Honour. Unfortunately, as I stated my practice with respect to objecting is to allow the flow of questions and answer to proceed accordingly. Regrettably yesterday in part -- I think it was page 68 of the transcript, if I'm not mistaken, Mr. Koumjian asked the question, which was a compound question, which also included the language when he was inquiring as to this witness's discussion with the Defence team, and he referenced to the extent -- I'm paraphrasing it, but I think I have it accurate. He was asked to testify to items that the Defence would allow him to testify to, the items that the Defence would like you to testify to. Again, I think it's an inappropriate question. It's not a question of the Defence wishing him. He came here as a witness to testify. And we believe he did give much testimony, as we know from the two days. It's that reference that I would hope that the OTP does not continue to ask our witnesses. Not if they met with the Defence or when they met with the Defence, but not to suggest that the Defence would in any manner manipulate or seek somehow to distort the testimony of witnesses. They are under oath and know their obligations once they take that oath. The Court has warned numerous witnesses in connection with their obligation. The Defence objects to the OTP suggesting that the Defence attorneys or our investigators would in any manner suggest to witnesses to provide certain answers. So we just for the record would like to make that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have heard this objection, but we have to come back to this later when we have the necessary time to discuss whether or not the proffers provided by the Defence orally and in writing were, in fact, misleading and brought this Trial Chamber to a decision which would not have been the outcome of our discussion whether or not a witness is relevant and -- but this concern has to be expressed in the presence of both Defence counsel. The Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to raise two matters, and one deals with the proffers, but perhaps it's better to deal with that, as Your Honour suggested, in the presence of both Defence counsel. But we were particularly concerned with the proffer of one of the upcoming witnesses. I believe it's number 45, that's being an example of an inadequate proffer. Even if that is accurate, it's just inadequate as far as the detail provided. But we're prepared to proceed for the rest of this week. The other matter I just wanted to raise briefly is that we did inform the Defence regarding one of the witnesses who previously testified who the Defence in their motion identified as a person that they would have had other questions for had they had the Rule 68 material submitted by the Prosecution in the summons interviews. And that's Mr. Marcelovic. I just want to remind the Defence that he is here today. He's here this week. And he's available this week to answer further relevant questions, if the Court finds that there are relevant questions arising from the material that was provided to the Defence after Mr. Marcelovic testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. But I deliberately didn't ask this question because I take it that having received the letter by the Prosecution in due time, it would be for the Defence to indicate if there -- they believe there is a necessity to hear a witness again, to cross-examine a witness again. And the same holds true for the two witnesses to come in January. I take it that the Defence does not have the intention to restart the cross-examination of the three persons mentioned in the same letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If the Court recalls, on December 3rd, 2002, the OTP sent us a letter which identified only one witness, Witness Q, that was going to be present this week to testify. That did relate to our motion for a mistrial, it was denied by the Court. At that time we responded, namely on December 4th, 2002, and suggested that we do feel there is a need. Upon consultation with Dr. Stakic and the rest of the Defence team, we determined, based upon the evidence that was produced to us following the Rule 68 disclosures, namely of those five individuals and specifically of the one and that the Court, I think, is well aware of, we decided not to question Witness Q. Subsequent to that - although on the same day, we believe, perhaps the 4th of December - we received another letter from the OTP identifying three additional witnesses with dates upon which they're expected to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We immediately responded to the first letter, Witness Q, which the Court referenced. The Defence likewise respond to the second letter, which identified these three individuals. Within that letter, based upon my recollection, we requested that we would like to re-examine the witness that is here this week. Actually, it was Witness number 21. I'm not sure if he was a private witness. I could identify him in the letter he was identified. So I don't believe that he is a private witness, and the OTP is nodding, it is a public witness, Muharem Murselovic. We do want to question Mr. Murselovic again. Based on the 68 disclosures of the members -- or purported members of the Crisis Staff in 1992. And that's what we indicated to the OTP at that time, and we also carbon copied the Court specifically with respect to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Court is only in the possession of the letter I mentioned before, as of 4 December 2002, mentioning three witnesses, one of them being in The Hague on 11 December. And as opposed to the other letter of the same date, we didn't receive any reaction from the Defence. We took it that it's not your intention to continue with the cross-examination of this witness. But if necessary, we can react immediately. But then, please, take into account that what we stated earlier: You have to demonstrate that on the basis of concrete questions that you weren't able to put these concrete questions to the witnesses when they had been here in The Hague and that these new questions are emanating from the statements missing at that point in time, I have never seen an answer related to Witness Murselovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, we can check with the registrar. We did file with the registry a letter responding specifically to the letter of the 4th of December, 2003 [sic], and we copied the Court. I'll check with the registry. The OTP, I believe, is in possession of that letter and we filed it the same day that we did the other letter, and I believe it was the 4th of December, 2002. Within that letter, we asked and identified and put on notice the OTP and the Court that we would like to discuss the issue and we are seeking leave to continue to question the witness. The Court has never set parameters as to how far in advance we should outline our specific questions of the witness. I'm prepared, having reviewed his summary in part this morning, to advise the Court the areas in which I'd like to touch upon with Mr. Murselovic. In that same letter, just by memory, I specifically state that with the remaining two witnesses - and the Defence reserves our right on this - with the remaining two witnesses, since they'll be called sometime in mid-January, that we notified the OTP - and it's outlined specifically in that letter that we submitted to the registry, to the OTP, carbon copying each of the three Judges - that we reserve our right at that time upon further evaluation to determine whether we will be asking questions of the remaining two individuals. I just don't want to record to reflect that we did not respond. We did respond. We responded in writing. It was filed in the normal channels. The Defence cannot and does not follow up to see if the Court did or did not receive that letter. We're confident it was received by the OTP because we talked about it. We were confident since our prior filings were always received that that one likewise would be given to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to inform counsel, that I'm not aware that we received the letter. I know the OTP is a large institution. Ms. Karper is not aware of it and Ms. Sutherland is not aware of it. Ms. Korner is away, so I'm not sure of whether it's possible that that letter somehow got to her office without reaching us. But none of us are aware of the receipt of a letter from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask Madam Registrar whether there was a letter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will double-check, Your Honour, if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are taken by surprise, admittedly. We are discussing this -- the issue what witness to be heard the next day, day by day, and you had possibilities enough to address this issue orally. If you believe you have written a letter, then you could have done it orally in addition. If you were under the impression that the Chamber has not received and not responded to your letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So but let's -- let's not discuss. Let's cross-check immediately. The Chamber is prepared to rule on your letter, whether the threshold is met, indicated in the hearing of 25 November 2002, and we are prepared to proceed with this witness today. Hopefully he has not yet left The Hague. May I ask the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: He has not left The Hague. And I'll have Ms. Karper try to arrange to make sure he doesn't leave today or tomorrow until we hear an answer from the Court. We'll notify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this, because this has priority, and we would find a possibility to hear, if necessary, this witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I do have one other brief matter. Just to ask the Defence if the order -- the witnesses for the first week, we were given them in the order of their 65 ter number, realising that things can change. Is this the, at the moment at least, the intended order in which they will be called? It would be helpful to us, and I'm sure, the Court to have some idea of the order of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We believe that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may I ask -- I just saw it, it reads the first week of January. Please recall the order was related to the first working -- the first eight working days of January 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. If the Court recalls, we start, I believe, on the 8th of January, which is three days of that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So we wouldn't have envisioned to call one of those witnesses. So that does -- it is for that first eight- to ten-day period, work-day period in January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. I can't see any other administrative matters, so therefore may I ask the usher, please, to escort the witness into the courtroom. May I ask Madam Registrar to be prepared to present document S169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness DD. Please be seated. This is a totally different environment, but the same holds true. You are still protected in the same way as it was during the last two days. And no doubt you are still under solemn declaration. May I ask you before starting the first -- with the first questions, do you want to add anything to your testimony of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness. The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What's the problem? The interpreters cannot hear the witness. Is it resolved now? May I ask you once again to try and find out whether the mic is working now. Do you want to add anything to your testimony of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness say something, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you try once again to answer the question whether or not you want to add something to your testimony of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to -- I would just like to add something in response to a question that was asked of me yesterday during my testimony in connection with the name of the person who held -- or actually holds a responsible function, a responsible office in the relevant ministry. Was that your question more or less? It is possible that I didn't understand the question. I mean, I think I said I didn't know, but maybe the question was who the first man in the police is in the relevant ministry, the entity ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My question was related to the name of the prosecutor general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Questioned by the Court: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness DD, in 1992 you were the age of 22, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you like to play soccer in your youth, or football?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not much of a sportsman, not much of a football player, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever been to the Ljubija football stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And can you explain the environment. Was there only a football place as such? Was there an area for other athletes as well? Was there a building for the athletes? Please try to give us a short overview of what you recall as the football stadium of Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't need to recall. It is situated in the immediate vicinity of my house, and there is an adjacent building which was used before as a changing room for athletes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You said "which was used before." And I think you covered already --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is still used for the same purpose, the ground floor, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And in the meantime, was it used for other purposes as well, this building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, it functioned as the seat of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The entire building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess. The building is not very large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you been in this building during the time you were mobilised, as you said, "about seven days in 1992"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have an opportunity to be there. This was not my -- the seat where I had to go. Or rather, there was no need for me to be there, even if I had an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And so was the sports grounds, as such, when the changing rooms were used by the forces you mentioned before, was it possible to play football or soccer in this area, on the place as such?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that it was possible to use it for this purpose, but nobody cared much about football in those days. There were no physical obstacles at the stadium. Even in those days, it was still open on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What do you mean by "open on both sides"? Is it your testimony that there was no fence around the football stadium as such?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was open. One side of the football stadium -- on one side of the football stadium is a forest, and there is no fence on that side -- or rather, there is some kind of fence, but it is not a continuous fence. There are gaps in it, and that's how it is today, as far as I know. As for the lower part of the football stadium, there used to be a fence which is actually still there, but it also has a gap -- a 10-metre gap approximately, and this is all very visible, because the fence itself is transparent. It is just a wire mesh fence. On the side of the road the area is not that visible. You cannot see the stadium with the naked eye. You can see the adjacent building though. And the upper side of the stadium also has an adjacent building, which is connected to the fence on the upper side, and it has a large entrance gate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are covered three sides. What about the fourth? Was there a fence or was there a wall or something similar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have described all four sides; one side being the wood, the lower side, the fence with gaps, the side next to the road as I said is not that visible. The stadium is not visible from the side of the road with the naked eye; only the adjacent building. And the fourth side consists of this other adjacent building. I believe I was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Also, you cannot see the stadium from the upper side with the naked eye except when the gate is open. It's not only my opinion; it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there a wall on one side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a wall on the side of the road, which I described. This is the physical obstacle that blocks the view of the stadium and the stands, which are situated in the middle of the stadium and are somewhat higher than the fence. That is the area that I said was not visible with the naked eye. And also, from the upper side, you cannot see the stadium except for when the gate is opened. You cannot see it through this adjacent building that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was this football stadium to the best of your recollection, living very close to this area, ever used as a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know was that at the time persons were taken there to be interviewed. As for any lengthy stay, no, I don't think that there was any talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were they brought to the building or to the football ground as such for this, as you called it -- in order to be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were brought both to the building and to the area next to the football pitch. Although, I never entered the premises at that time. I was never there. This is what I heard from other people, when talking to other people. But I personally never visited the area. I was never there, so I cannot give you a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever hear shooting from this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see corpses in this area after the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't. Shooting could be heard even during the day and during the night intermittently, which doesn't necessarily mean that people were being killed. Though, I do not know the real answer, because I was never there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From your answer, I take it that you speak about people that -- "they were brought to this area." Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what is --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I indicated that people were sometimes brought there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the usher to present Exhibit number S169 to the witness. And may it be -- please be put on the ELMO. Could you please be so kind with the help of a marker to indicate where you lived in 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Ljubija here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the usher please bring a dark marker to the witness that you can mark your place of residence on this map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Is this enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. And the football stadium was where, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the photograph or on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the map, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, in this area, in the area of Ljubija town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You have marked the place of your own residence by a cross. Could you please mark the place of the football stadium with a circle on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is my place of residence, then the stadium is here approximately. It -- the map is much too small for me to indicate the distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. And may this Exhibit number S169 with the additional marks on it be called S169A, so that we know the source of these additional marks. May I ask you, when you have the car before you, did you ever drive with your [redacted] to Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No not to Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: With your own car to Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the war operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Had you ever heard about a checkpoint between Brisevo and Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several roads between Brisevo and Ljubija that can be used. I didn't know them. I never went to Brisevo in those days. I never had an opportunity to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. For the moment we don't need any longer this special map. In the beginning of your testimony in chief, you mentioned that there were several camps for different purposes, as you stated. What would you call a camp in this sense in the area of the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: What camp exactly do you have in mind or generally speaking, the notion of a camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we were clear enough when we discussed Omarska and then you made a distinction opposed to Trnopolje. Were there other to the best of your recollection, let's call it detention facilities, detention buildings -- you mentioned in the connection with the football stadium that this place was used for the purpose of interviewing civilians. Were there other such places you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje, where people were detained for longer periods of time. And I also said the Ljubija football stadium, when people were kept there, they were kept there only for very short, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And you recall no other place in the municipality of Prijedor serving for the same purposes as, for example, the football stadium and Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I really understand that it was difficult for you on the basis of a small picture to identify Omarska. May the usher please present document S15-18 to the witness, and please put it on the ELMO. Does this reproduction assist you in finding out from which side you approached Omarska at that time, when you drove there with the second-last bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that it could not assist me. I was there for the first time next to this big building, and I recognised the area according to the photograph, but it was ten years ago, so I don't remember. And I only stayed there very briefly. And I'm not familiar enough with the area anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it is your testimony that you saw only the building from outside and you have no own direct knowledge what happened inside the building, what happened on the entire area depicted here on this still? Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I stated yesterday, and I still abide by what I said because I stood only at the gate of the compound. I didn't stray away from the bus. I didn't go inside the buildings at all, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And to come back to another question I put to you yesterday: Having discussed now Ljubija football stadium, Omarska, Trnopolje, what would be your categorisation of Keraterm? What was the purpose of Keraterm in 1992 from the perspective of a civilian living in the municipality of Prijedor and for professional purposes, sometimes driving to Prijedor and being in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I know about the Keraterm camp. I know that its purpose was to have an opportunity to control a certain number of civilians in one place. The implication being that they did not go there on their own free will. I don't know if this is enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And you knew this in 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about this on account of the stories that I heard. I never had a chance to get closer to the camp or visit the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Correct. This is what I understood from your testimony. But you heard about that already in 1992 from other persons telling you stories they have heard from Keraterm, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this was only after a lot of people had already been released from Omarska and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you in this connection another question: On page 61, line 23 of Monday's transcript, you immediately answered, when only being there for an extremely short period of time at Omarska, what was the reason for you to ask whether the persons being there were "physically or mentally mistreated"? What brought you to this question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked that question in Trnopolje, as far as I recall, and not in Omarska. And I didn't have an opportunity to contact anyone in Omarska, anyone from the civilians who were already detained there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But then let me repeat the same question in relation to Trnopolje: What was the reason? Why did you ask this question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the individuals in Trnopolje? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: For purposes of information. I wanted to see how they were treated, what was the treatment generally speaking. I don't think it was a stupid question at the time. And it was not ill-intentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I know that you answered this question already, the one and the other time, but I have to come back to this. Is it correct that all in all three of your relatives were in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two relatives and one friend, and a few acquaintances, some of whom I knew better than others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would be your estimate, the number of persons all in all who you knew at the time being in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hard for me to say. I really can't give you an answer to that question. I knew quite a few people there, but I wouldn't be able to give you their exact number. It would be wrong to say that I didn't know those people, especially those who were from Ljubija itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But did you know about the ethnicity of these persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course. Ljubija is a relatively small place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And so were they Serbs? Were they Croats, or Muslims predominantly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims were detained in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned that it was possible for you to bring the one or other person back to their homes when released from Trnopolje. What about the three persons you mentioned just beforehand, the two relatives and the one friend? They were all released on the basis of Serbian guarantees? Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered that question to the Prosecutor, if I can remember. I took my friend home personally. I don't know who signed the release documents for him. His wife kept it a secret. She came with me to pick him up. At the end of the day, I wasn't that interested in finding out who had signed the document. The most important thing was for him to go home, obviously. As for one of my uncles, it was my father who was the guarantor, and he escorted him home. I don't know how they then went to Prijedor, and from Prijedor to Ljubija they travelled on a local bus which had already started running between the two places. And the third person, my other uncle, got the guarantee from a taxi driver whom I don't know. I only know that there was some compensation, some money involved in that. And that same taxi driver brought my uncle home. My uncle never told me how much he had to pay for that. He always shrugged it off and always said, "It doesn't really matter. What matters is that I'm now home." That is what I know personally about these three men. I don't know about others, whether they had to have the written guarantees of relatives, Serbs, friends, Serbs, or maybe they had to pay for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you: Did you ever discuss with these three persons, especially with those you escorted home yourself, about that what happened to them and to others in Trnopolje? Did they speak about any beatings or other violence vis-a-vis detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't tell me. I did ask them, and they said that during the short time that they had been in Trnopolje, nothing like that had happened. So we didn't talk much about that period of time. I didn't really find it necessary to talk too much about that. The most important thing was that they were home, that they were free. And now, after so much time has gone by, we really don't talk about it. It never occurs to us to reminisce on those times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But wouldn't you yourself find it surprising that when coming first to such a camp, you immediately asked what about "physical or mental mistreatment"? And then, later on having the possibility to discuss this with your relative and friend, or you didn't discuss this at all? Is really your testimony under solemn declaration that you never discussed these questions and you never heard about beatings and other kind of violence in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the first time I met with them, I asked them how they were, how they were treated. I said that yesterday and the day before. They answered, "The conditions are not ideal. The food is not good. Their accommodation is very poor. Some sleep on beds, some sleep on the floor." And they also said that nobody was beating them or otherwise ill-treating them. That's what my cousins told me later on when we got home. We never discussed it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And you never discussed with them the name of Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe then at that time, but not later on. If we don't talk about things, we can't mention any names, can we? If they don't want to talk about it, if they do not want to dwell upon it, why should I insist on that? Why should I be interested in talking about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Quite clear. But you answered, "Maybe then at that time." You are under solemn declaration, and I have to insist, please answer the question. Did you discuss the name of -- the personality of Mr. Kuruzovic with one or all the three of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. It was a long time ago. It was ten years ago. I really did not expect such questions, which doesn't imply that I'm not prepared to answer them. I myself mentioned Trnopolje. Already the day before yesterday I told you how I got there the first time, the second time, and the third time. If the Defence counsel had not asked me that, I would have mentioned it anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My final question would be: Who do you believe was not the Urije, but on the basis of the title, the main political responsible person in Prijedor municipality and on what factual basis do you come to this assessment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer to that. I know that there were some military officers as representatives of the military. One of them was Colonel Arsic. Then there was Radmilo Zeljaja. I believe that his rank was also colonel. The late Simo Drljaca, who was the chief of the police. And there were also people from the civilian authorities. Those people had most influence at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So that the transcript is clear and unambiguous, it reads now, "There were also people from the civilian authorities. Those people had most influence at that time." Could you please comment on this. And as you did it in relation to military personnel, what were the persons in civilian authorities you recall at that time, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Mr. Srdjo Srdic, for example. Allegedly he was a representative in the People's Assembly. There was also Mr. Simo Miskovic. I don't know what his position was. The late Dr. Kovacevic. Again, I don't know what his position was at the time. These -- this is my answer, but I only learnt that later on, after the war. At that time I was not aware of all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally, in -- when you escorted the bus on its way first to Omarska and then to Prijedor, in which capacity did you act at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the road first to Omarska and then to Trnopolje, not to Prijedor, I was an escort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And we learned that you were at that time [redacted] [redacted]. Did you act as [redacted]--

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And who asked you to act as [redacted] and why was it necessary to have [redacted]acting as an escort on a bus to a camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted], but I was off duty. My shift was 48 hours, and then I would be off for the following 48 hours. On that particular day I was off duty and one of the military came by my house and saw me, saw me that I was free, that I wasn't doing anything. I can't remember who it was. They had already seen the other [redacted] performing his regular duties. Then they ordered me to come with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And you volunteered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went for purely safety reasons, for my own safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that you were compelled to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say I was compelled or forced to go. They simply told me, "You are coming with us." I could have refused, but I feared the possible consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So taking all the time together you spent there in the Brdo area when the targeted persons were collected and brought to the buses and then brought first in part to Omarska and then later to Trnopolje, how many hours did this take from the first bus to the last bus? You told us that you observed this entire exodus.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that operation lasted from approximately 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning until 3.00 in the afternoon. But I arrived later, and then I got on my bus. I did not participate in the operation of gathering people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Witness DD, you testified about three incidents, the incident in Hambarine, Kozarac, and Prijedor, which took place between the 22nd of May -- 22nd of May and 30th of May, 1992. Where had you been when these incidents occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: At home. The third incident happened on the 30th of May. That is when I was for the first time assigned to provide a security for the police building in Ljubija, on that same evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Next question: Did you personally know at least some persons involved in these incidents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that I knew some people in the first incident, that is, on the 21st of May. And as for the others, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And whom did you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the persons who fell victim to the accident in the car on the 21st of May. I didn't know all of them. I knew three of them, three of the six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Can you name them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sinisa Mijatovic, who was injured; Miroslav Lulic, who is now dead. He subsequently committed suicide. And Nedeljko Antunovic. I believe that he was also injured at that time -- I'm sorry, Sinisa Mijatovic and Ratko Milojica were injured. I didn't know Ratko Milojica at the time. I also didn't know the late Lukic and the other Milojica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Did these persons belong to the army or the police or paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Next question: While visiting Trnopolje camp for the second time with the purpose to see your friend, had you a chance to contact your relatives detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I did have contacts with all of them, with both my cousins and the friend, and I've already said it. I've said it several times. And I've already told you what we were talking about, what was the reason for which I went there. I did have contacts with them. I told them how they were, how they were treated, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And one more on the last question: Have you or your father ever tried to reach municipal authorities in order to get your relatives released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. And as for my father, I don't know. I can't speak for my father. I only know that my father put his name on the guarantee for one of my uncles. I really can't tell you who he might have contacted. I really don't know. This wasn't important at the time. The most important thing for us was for my relatives to get home. How this was to be done was of minor importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Very well. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I have two or three very simple questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I hope you can that answer very shortly. As a person who has done your military service, were you aware that the army had barracks in Prijedor and that that was the place for a brigade who was first number 43, I think, and then 143, and then 343? Were you aware of the existence of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the existence of that brigade. The barracks were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Just stop there. And then I'll continue. Because if not, you are going to give an explanation that I don't need. Do you know how many men composed that brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There were also reserve soldiers who had been mobilised, so I wouldn't be able to give you the number of the men in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. More or less. Would you tell me there were 500, 1000, more than 1000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't tell you. I don't know the number. Whatever I might tell you, I'm afraid would be wrong. I know that the brigade was rather large. And given the fact that it was a brigade -- a brigade usually has a certain number of men in it. It has a certain strength. I don't know how much it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Then just turning to those episodes or those events that you were talking earlier in your testimony just some days ago. You told us for the incident in Hambarine of the name and number of soldiers that were wounded or dead. And then after, you told us about the driver who was killed in the Kozarac - I'm sorry for the pronunciation of the names - in the Kozarac incident two days afterwards. And then you told us that there was a false -- an attack by Bosniak forces on Prijedor on May 30th. Correct? And you said that this force that attacked Prijedor was around 200 men. You told us so, this in the transcript on the first day. And I want to ask you: Do you know - you were very well informed over these events and the incidents - do you know what arms this group of 200 men had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they had their personal infantry long-barrel weapons or side weapons. I really don't know. They had automatic weapons, semi-automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Did they have tanks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be sure about trucks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Rockets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rockets and zoljas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. And the last one, if I may: Do you remember what road did you take from your city to Prijedor hospital when you were driving some ill person to Prijedor? Do you remember the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's just one road. There is just that one shortest route from my place to Prijedor, which is about 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. And inside the city of Prijedor, you have the same road to go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through Prijedor there are obviously several streets one can take. I mostly took one way or one route. If I had a map, I could show you that that route went by Prijedor hotel, by the Orthodox church, by a place called Ereza. Then the police building, the building of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then on towards Ravno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: That's enough. Just listening to you, and you just answer my next question, that you passed the police offices building on your way to the Prijedor hospital. Have you ever seen queues of people in front of that building in the period we are talking about? That means -- you were [redacted] [redacted] from June 1992 on. Let's say from June 1992 to September 1992, have you ever seen queues of people -- lines of people in front of the police building in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The words [redacted]please be redacted from the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand your question, but I can't remember. I can't give you an answer to this question. Maybe I didn't pay too much attention to any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask Defence counsel, any questions in re?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then before we have the break, we need some clarification. Did we find out whether or not there was such a letter as indicated by Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We found a copy of a letter that was sent on the 4th of December. Apparently it was in Ms. Korner's office and apparently it was delivered after she was away. I'll give the Court our copy. And I do have some comments about the contents, but it will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But we have to -- immediately to decide whether or not this witness can leave The Hague or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, I would just indicate briefly that that witness is not mentioned in the letter. Two other witnesses are, and that witness is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What is the response by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know I spoke to Ms. Joanna Korner on Friday of last week. I know that she received my correspondence. I know that I faxed them to the registry and copied the Court, specifically responding to the two letters I received from the OTP. If the Court even examines the December 4th, 2002, letter, it has one name initially, and that is Witness Q. We responded in kind with respect to Witness Q. Subsequently, we received another fax. It was not addressed to anyone personally. It starts with -- the introduction, sir, is we specifically and I specifically recall that we addressed it directly to Ms. Korner, because she's the one who gave us the letter. In response -- what we did was respond to Witness Q and thereafter respond with respect to the two witnesses who will be brought in early or mid-January 2003. We responded also with respect to Witness number 21, Muharem Murselovic, and spoke with Ms. Joanna Korner specifically about that. I believe it was Thursday evening or Friday evening when I met with her when she exchanged the tapes of the Rule 68 disclosures in B/C/S so that our client for the first time can have access to review them. At that time I informed her, as I'm sure that she'll recall, that we will not be seeking, having spoken with our client and the rest of the Defence team, to be speaking further questions from Witness Q. Likewise, at that time, I informed her that we would, if this witness, who is scheduled to arrive on the 11th of December, based upon my recollection, in order to commence his testimony in the Brdjanin trial. He was going to be here mid-week this week. And had indicated to her that we would have some questions, if permitted by the Court, to address that. Also, when we were asked specifically in connection with this, these issues, the Court asked me on Monday specifically in connection with Witness Q, who apparently, according to the letter had representations made to us, was arriving that week, scheduled to testify. It was not a question that the witness was going to be testifying on one day and immediately leave the day after. Nevertheless, we informed Ms. Korner we think in ample time that we would not be seeking her testimony any further in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. We don't want to reopen discussion of the past. We are discussing now in concreto Witness Muharem Murselovic. And it reads from the letter by -- from the Prosecution, addressed to Mr. Branko Lukic and to Mr. John Ostojic that this person would be available on 11 December, and the threshold has been indicated several times to the Defence. So may I ask you: Is it your intention to hear Mr. Murselovic today and on the basis of which questions? I don't have anything in writing, and it's really surprising to find out that we have two answers from your side making reference to the three others but not to Mr. Murselovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically, we addressed that in our correspondence to the OTP, as well as orally. Our letter was almost identical as theirs was in response to Witness Q. Surprising to me that the Court doesn't have it. I sent the letters out personally. With respect to Witness Murselovic, we would like to ask him questions based upon information that we learned from the Rule 68 tapes. Mr. Murselovic, as the Court may know, stated on page 2.675 of his testimony that he was active politically within the municipality of Prijedor and was an assemblyman. His name is also mentioned within some of the individuals that were the Rule 68 disclosures known to them personally of this witness. They can enlighten us or he can enlighten us, since he continues to testify on page 2.815 of his deposition -- of his testimony that he considers the first three to be the most powerful politicians in Prijedor. I would like to ask him further questions regarding those three people which he identifies on page 2.815 - and this is a summary that I'm reading from. I apologise if it's not directly accurate, but I believe that it is quite accurate -- he identifies Simo Miskovic, Dragan Savanovic, and Srdjo Srdic. Those three individuals who have provided the OTP with interviews, I would like to ask Mr. Murselovic further questions about those three individuals, as well as further questions regarding his relationship while an elected assemblyman in Prijedor during the same time that these individuals were also elected assemblymen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I hereby invite one representative of each party and a representative of the registrar for 4.00 sharp in my office. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 9659 to 9662. We have to continue with the re-examination of the Witness DD. And for this purpose, the trial stays adjourned until twenty minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we continue with the re-examination of Witness DD, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I ask you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further examination by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DD, I have a couple of points that I'd like to perhaps clarify with you for my own purposes. Can I ask you when was the first time that you first learned of the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when the military activity was going on in the month of June 1992, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, if you will, did you learn anything else about that facility, such as whether things were taking place there, violent things, at or about that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at that time that I heard of the Keraterm camp, but I learned later on that there had been violence as well on the part of irresponsible individuals. I believe I stated that yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- and I apologise if you did state it yesterday. I don't have it necessarily in my notes. Tell me when you learned, given the month and the year, of any violence that may have occurred at the Keraterm detention centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the end of 1992 when people were -- some of the people were released home from Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it fair to say that prior to that time you did not learn or hear of any such activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did. I don't know how long those persons were in Keraterm. I don't know when it ceased to operate. I'm not sure whether it was in late summer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, with the Court's permission, Witness DD, a question asked by Your Honour regarding responsible persons in the Prijedor municipality. Now, you mentioned several military and police, and then you mentioned several of the civilian authorities, and you also suggested, I believe, based on my notes, that those persons were most influential. Can you help me understand that answer and tell me who, sir, did you mean when you stated "those persons were most influential." Which persons are you talking about, the military, the police, civilian, all three, or any combination of the three?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume I meant the persons who held the most responsible functions, including the military, police functions. I did hear about civilians as well. I stated their names. I didn't know any of them personally. I heard that they held certain responsible functions, offices within the municipal civilian structure. I don't know exactly what offices they had. I heard that Mr. Srdjo Srdic was the deputy of the National Assembly. I knew about his function. I didn't know about the other two. And obviously these individuals had more authority than myself and other ordinary citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final question, if I may. Having lived there and made the observations that you shared with us, can you tell me which of those three in your opinion, sir, would have the most influence as to what was going on and occurring in Prijedor in the spring and summer of 1992? Namely, was it the military that had the most influence as to those action or crimes that were committed, the political establishment, the politicians, or the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume if you're talking about the conflict at the beginning of the war, that it must have been the military that had the most influence. It was the soldiers who took people into custody. I never heard of any civilian having taken anyone to custody or to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just a few questions following up. Further cross-examination by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you discussed with His Honour Judge Schomburg the trip to Omarska and the route that you took. That bus trip from the Brdo area to Omarska, you arrived on a regular paved road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an asphalt road connecting Rizvanovici and Biscani and Prijedor and further on towards Omarska. And we took the main road to go to Omarska, in the direction of Banja Luka. At Nisevici we turned towards Omarska - I don't know to what extent you're familiar with the area - and we came back from Omarska and then to Trnopolje via Petrov Gaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding the military police that were guarding the stadium at Ljubija, can you tell us the uniforms that they wore, what those uniforms looked like.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were military uniforms. Some had camouflage uniforms and some had plain olive-drab uniforms, the so-called SMB uniform with white belts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you escorted the bus to Omarska and Trnopolje were you given a uniform and a weapon; one or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had, as far as I can remember, the upper part of my clothing was olive-grey, and I had camouflage trousers that I had taken from my father, because I had not been issued with these military uniforms. And I also had my father's rifle with me, the one that he had been given as a member of the reserve military force, because I didn't have any personal weapons at the time, any long-barrel weapon, rifle, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are we in private session any just want to double-check. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, so it's correct, isn't it, that during 1992 there were people of Serb nationality -- there were many people of Serb nationality who tried to protect their Muslim and Croat neighbours, who disagreed with the persecutions and the crimes that were happening against them? This wasn't the Serbian people of Prijedor doing this. This was specific individuals. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume not the person who signed the papers of their own free will. Maybe those who had some interest in signing such documents, they -- they did that. There are all kinds of people, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe I wasn't clear, but there were many people, many Serbian people, who disagreed with the crimes against their neighbours and who tried to protect Muslim and Croat neighbours, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were such people. I don't know their number. I wouldn't be able to tell you the percentage either. I don't personally know any such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, though, that the atmosphere was such in Prijedor and the atmosphere with the authorities that it was understandable that a woman, like the one we just spoke about in private session, would want to keep that name of that particular person who had helped her secret, because for some people, for some Serbs it was dangerous for it to be known that they helped their neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess that it was so. I don't know why they kept it secret. Again, as I said, I was not interested in knowing that. What was important was for this friend to be able to go back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your position that you've talked about, the power of the military, it's your position, as I understand it, that the military could choose who would be the leader of the civilian government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that it was the military who took over in a peaceful way, and it is my assumption, which does not have to be correct, that they were in the position to elect the civilian authorities until somebody would be put in that position. That's my assumption. I wouldn't be able to tell you the correct -- or the appropriate answer. If the military was influential, especially some of its officers, then they might have had influence on the civilian authorities as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand you've been testifying based upon your assumptions of what was occurring in Prijedor. So you would assume that if a civilian leader was not cooperating, the military would have removed that leader, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It may have been so. From the position that I am in, I wouldn't be able to tell you. As for Dr. Stakic, maybe it wasn't the military who appointed him. Maybe it was not the military who told him, "You're just going to be a figure person and you're going to have to say whatever -- do whatever we tell you to do." I don't know whether it -- whether that happened in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of public interviews by Colonel Arsic, television interviews, for example, where he said he kept the civilian authorities very well informed about military matters in Prijedor, and are you aware of public interviews by Dr. Stakic where he indicated that cooperation between the civilian and military authorities in Prijedor was very good?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with such interviews. I've already told you that I was not interested in the media, especially immediately upon the breakout of the war. I wasn't following the media almost at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a person living in Prijedor, during the period from May through September of 1992, did you see any evidence, and if so, please explain it to us, any evidence of conflict between the military, police, and civilian authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any such evidence. I wasn't interested in the political situation. I wasn't into politics at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions. Just for the Court's information, the interview -- okay. Sorry. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This concludes the testimony of Witness DD. May I finally ask you: Did you, when coming to The Hague, feel under some pressure by whomsoever to be quite precise? This is not related at all to the Defence -- but under pressure of other persons living together with you in Ljubija or other persons you are working with or you're a subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us hear the answer in closed session -- in not closed session. It will be too difficult. In private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be heard. The Defence has a position. We would like it in open session. Just, I want on the record to note our position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the witness: Do you believe it would help you to answer the question truthfully when we hear your answer in private session? Will it assist you in answering my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can easily give it in an open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not experience any political pressures either in my institutions -- institution where I work or by any of my neighbours, citizens of Ljubija, or anybody else. I came here of my own will, nobody persuaded me to come here -- and "here," I mean the gentlemen from the Defence, regardless of the circumstances that may have prevented me from coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You only should know that whenever you feel it necessary to add something or to clarify something, it is open for you to contact the Court in writing or through the Defence if you feel it necessary. Thank you for coming. This concludes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour, ask if the Court cares to inquire. The OTP would like to permission of the witness to disclose his transcript in other cases, specifically the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you understand the question? Do you agree that your transcript is used as well in one or other cases, especially the case Prosecutor versus Mr. Brdjanin in order to avoid that you have to appear a second time here in The Hague? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is up to you, Your Honours, to decide whether my testimony is relevant. As I've already told you, I'm here of my own will to help the Honourable Court to come to the truth regardless of the final outcome of this procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. You didn't answer my question. Do you agree that your testimony is used in other cases on the basis of the transcript you can see before you as well? This is one rule aiming at -- that the witness has not to appear another time in The Hague. Do you agree that this transcript, that what is written down from your testimony, is used in other cases as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that the transcript will protect my identity. And if that is the case, I don't have any objections to the transcript being used as an exhibit in any other trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then this is accepted under the same protective measures as applicable during this testimony. Thank you for coming. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. Wait a moment. Is my understanding that also the next witness appears under pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be then DE. And also voice and face distortion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to make a correction, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll reopen the testimony of Witness DD. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to make a correction about my personal data. The Defence counsel asked me the day before yesterday about my marital status, and my answer was that I was married and a father of one child. Are we still in private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. But if need may be and there are no objections - I don't believe - then we'll go, please, in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: During the break, in the framework of a 65 ter (I) meeting, the minutes will follow. We discussed the question of whether or not to hear Witness Murselovic another time in this case. The factual basis is the following: That it is a submission of the Defence and we have no reasonable doubts - that is a fact - that the Defence has sent another letter to the Office of the Prosecutor and asking for copies to be sent to the Judges. We didn't receive the second letter, and we didn't receive the third letter, but -- and we didn't receive until now concrete questions, as we stated, the 25th of November, 2002, questions -- concrete questions to be demonstrated by the Defence that they were not able to put to the witnesses when they had been here in The Hague and that these new questions are emanating from the statements missing at that point in time.
